questions.q: How does Q#'s `use (q0, q1) = (Qubit(), Qubit())` differ from Qiskit's `QuantumCircuit(2, 2)` in terms of classical register handling?
options: They are identical -- both declare a separate classical register structure

Qiskit declares a quantum register AND a separate classical register up front; Q# allocates qubits dynamically with use, and has no separate classical register since measured Result values are just ordinary typed values
Q# requires declaring three separate registers instead of two
Qiskit does not support classical registers at all
questions.explain: Qiskit's constructor declares both quantum and classical registers as part of building the circuit object; Q# has no equivalent parallel classical register -- Result values returned from M are ordinary typed values.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between Qiskit's `.h(0)` / `.cx(0,1)` calls and Q#'s `H(q0)` / `CNOT(q0,q1)` calls?
options: There is no difference; both execute identically

Qiskit's calls append gate instructions to the circuit object's internal list (the circuit accumulates as data); Q#'s calls take effect immediately when executed, with no intermediate list being built
Q#'s calls can only be used once per program
Qiskit's calls execute immediately with no circuit object involved at all
questions.explain: This reflects the design-philosophy lesson from earlier in the chapter: Qiskit builds a circuit as mutable data (appending to a list), while Q# operations execute directly with no intermediate circuit-as-data representation.

questions.q: For the ported Bell-state circuit, what was the verified exact probability of measuring '01' or '10'?
options: 0.25 for each
Exactly 0 for each -- the Bell state has zero amplitude on both of those outcomes
0.5 for each
It cannot be determined without running on real hardware
questions.explain: Direct matrix computation of H-then-CNOT on |00> gives amplitude exactly 1/sqrt(2) on |00> and |11> only, with zero amplitude -- and therefore zero probability -- on |01> and |10>.

questions.q: How does Q# represent the measurement step compared to Qiskit's `.measure([0,1],[0,1])`?
options: Q# has no way to represent measurement at all
Q# returns the measured Result values directly as the operation's return value (e.g. a (Result, Result) tuple), rather than writing into indexed classical register slots read out later
Q# requires measurement to happen before any gates are applied
Both approaches are completely identical with no structural difference
questions.explain: Qiskit writes measurement outcomes into classical register slots, read from a results object afterward; Q# returns the Result values directly as the operation's own return type, matching its 'operation is the computation' model from earlier in the chapter.

questions.q: What is the actual pedagogical point of porting a circuit this small (2 gates), according to the lesson?
options: To prove that one of the two languages cannot express simple circuits
To make visible exactly where each tool's design philosophy shows up even in a minimal example, so that the same mapping scales to larger algorithms like Grover's or teleportation
To demonstrate that gate counts always differ between the two languages
To show that translation between the two tools is impossible without a specialized converter tool
questions.explain: The exercise is deliberately small so the translation decisions (register vs. allocation, append-to-list vs. direct call, indexed classical slot vs. typed return value) are easy to see individually, then apply the same mapping to larger, already-implemented algorithms.
